items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Single-letter names carry the business logic (`big a, b, c`, `long k`, struct fields `d, n, cap`). The language-switching trick (`#if 0` / `""" "`) has no comment in the file; it is only explained in the final message.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: Short functions: `big_add` is a separate helper and `main` is about 20 lines. Minor leftovers: `#include <string.h>` is never used, and the bignum code adds a lot of machinery the conventions didn't ask for.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: Return values of `realloc` and `calloc` are never checked. `strtol(argv[1], NULL, 10)` doesn't validate non-numeric input, so it prints 0. The Python side has no argument checking at all (`k = int(sys.argv[1])`), so a missing argument ends in a traceback and a negative N prints 0.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: Both sides give f(0)=0 and f(1)=1, both are iterative, and the C bignum is correct well past 93. But argument handling is incomplete: C prints 0 for non-numeric input, Python prints 0 for a negative N, and Python's missing-argument case is an uncaught IndexError rather than a usage message.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: Works with exactly the two given commands and no extra flags. It compiled cleanly even with `-Wall -Wextra`. Each run prints only the number. The C code inside the Python string has only valid escapes (`\n`), so Python emits no SyntaxWarning.
